passage:
Uma: we need to talk. I ran the numbers again last night
Usha: the investor said no?
Uma: second no this month. and we have 7 weeks of runway left
Usha: 😔 I was hoping the Pune pilot would change their mind
Uma: the pilot taught us something though. people loved the tiffins but only ordered on weekdays. weekends were empty
Usha: so paying for the kitchen on weekends was eating us alive
Uma: yes. I think we shut the subscription, pay the two cooks their full notice, and write down everything we learned
Usha: it feels like failing
Uma: it is failing. but we got 140 paying customers from a sheet on a gym noticeboard. that part worked
Usha: can I be sad for one day first
Uma: take two. then coffee on Thursday and we list what we'd do differently 🤍
Usha: ok. thank you for saying it straight

qa.q: How many weeks of runway were left?
qa.a: There were 7 weeks of runway left.

qa.q: What is Usha feeling about the shutdown?
qa.a: Usha feels sad and ashamed of failing, asking for a day to grieve before looking back.

qa.q: What makes Uma's shutdown plan a responsible one?
qa.a: It stops the loss-making subscription, pays the cooks their full notice, and sets a time to write down the lessons.

qa.q: What is it like for the two cooks when the venture closes?
qa.a: Losing the job is hard for them, but full notice gives them time and shows they were treated with respect.

grounding: Shows young founders facing failed fundraising and closing a venture while learning from it.

subtype: Reskilling & Career Change in an AI Era
passage: Leela, when my team at the call centre was cut from forty to twelve after the automated chat system came in, I thought I was next. I'd only ever done customer support, and I spent one full week refreshing job sites and feeling sick. Then my team lead said something that stuck: "You know our customers better than the software does." So I looked at what the new system actually needed. People to write the answers it gives, check where it goes wrong, and handle the angry cases it can't. I did a four-month evening course in writing help content, half paid for by the company. I made a sample by rewriting twenty of our worst bot replies. Today I, Arnab, lead the small team that trains that chat system. The fear hasn't gone. I just know how to keep learning now.

qa.q: How many people were left on Arnab's team after the cut?
qa.a: Twelve people were left, down from forty.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel in the week after the cuts?
qa.a: Arnab felt scared and sick with worry, refreshing job sites and expecting to be next.

qa.q: Which choice turned the threat into a new role for Arnab?
qa.a: Studying what the new system actually needed, taking a targeted course, and building a sample by rewriting the worst bot replies.

qa.q: How might the team lead see Arnab's change?
qa.a: The team lead likely feels proud and pleased, having pointed out that Arnab's customer knowledge was worth something.

grounding: Shows a young worker adapting to automation through deliberate retraining into a new role.

subtype: Conflict of Interest, Data Privacy & Honest Reporting
passage: Vishal, you know the quarterly report I kept complaining about? Here's what happened. Our app's sign-ups had dropped twelve percent, and my manager asked me to "find a better way to show it." He meant counting the test accounts our own team had created, which would have turned the drop into a small rise. The client pays us based on growth, and my appraisal was two weeks away. I actually built that chart. Then I looked at it and felt sick. So I made two versions: the real one with a note explaining the drop, and a page of fixes for the sign-up screen. I took both to the manager and said I couldn't send the padded one with my name on it. He was quiet for a long minute. Then he sent the real one. My appraisal was fine, by the way. Pradeep the troublemaker survived.

qa.q: By how much had sign-ups dropped?
qa.a: Sign-ups had dropped twelve percent.

qa.q: What did Pradeep feel after building the padded chart?
qa.a: Pradeep felt sick and uneasy, knowing the padded chart would mislead the client.

qa.q: Why was bringing two versions a wise move?
qa.a: It showed the honest numbers with an explanation and offered fixes, giving the manager a constructive alternative instead of a bare refusal.

qa.q: What might the manager have felt during that long silent minute?
qa.a: The manager may have felt torn and a bit ashamed, weighing client pressure against being called out, before choosing the honest report.

grounding: Shows a young professional refusing to inflate metrics and reporting data honestly under pressure.

passage: They had forty-eight hours to sign the lease on the Kochi flat, and Tanvir and Raghav still hadn't agreed on how to split anything. The broker kept calling. That evening the power went out in Raghav's building, so they sat on the stairs with a torch and a notebook. "I earn more," Raghav said. "I should pay more rent." Tanvir shook his head. "Then I'll feel like a guest." They tried another way: rent in proportion to income, a shared account for groceries and bills, each keeping their own savings. Cooking went to Raghav, who loved it; Tanvir took the laundry and the monthly paperwork. The harder question came last. "Your parents still think I'm your flatmate," Tanvir said quietly. Raghav was silent a while. "I'll tell them before we move. Together, if you'll come." Tanvir squeezed his hand. They signed the next morning.

qa.q: Which chore did Raghav take on?
qa.a: Cooking went to Raghav, who loved it.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir refuse to let Raghav simply pay more rent?
qa.a: Tanvir worried about feeling like a guest instead of an equal partner in their home.

qa.q: What helped them reach a fair arrangement under pressure?
qa.a: They tried a proportional split, a shared account for bills and separate savings, divided chores by preference, and faced the family question openly.

qa.q: What would change if Raghav kept the relationship hidden from his parents?
qa.a: Tanvir would likely keep feeling hurt and unseen in their shared life, and the secret could strain the partnership.

grounding: Shows a young couple negotiating money, chores and honesty with family before moving in together.

passage:
Dear Sangeeta Akka,
You asked last week whether Karthik and I are "planning anything yet," and I laughed it off. Here's the real answer.
We've started talking about it properly, not just "someday." We sat down with our budget and a list: what we'd change at work, who takes leave when, which of us is up at night. Karthik said he'd take a full month off, not the three days his father took. I cried a little at that, happy tears mostly.
But I'm also scared. I watched you after Anu was born, doing everything while your in-laws told you what you were doing wrong. I don't want that. We want to raise a child who argues politely and helps in the kitchen, whether a boy or a girl.
We're not ready yet. Maybe in a year. Can I call on Sunday and ask the questions nobody else answers honestly?
Love,
Yamini

qa.q: How long did Karthik say he would take off?
qa.a: He said he would take a full month off.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Yamini describe?
qa.a: Yamini feels happy and moved by Karthik's promise, but scared of repeating Sangeeta's lonely, criticised time after Anu was born.

qa.q: What steps show Yamini and Karthik preparing wisely?
qa.a: They talked through budget, leave and night duty, agreed to share care, and plan to ask Sangeeta honest questions before deciding.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel reading Yamini's memory of her early days with Anu?
qa.a: Sangeeta might feel understood and a little sad, touched that her hard time is helping Yamini plan differently 🤍

grounding: A young adult's letter reflects on readiness, money, values and sharing care before becoming a parent.

passage:
Vaibhav,
I'm writing instead of calling because I lose my temper on calls, and I don't want to this time.
Baba fell again on Tuesday. Not badly, a bruised wrist, but he was on the bathroom floor for twenty minutes before the neighbour heard him. I've been going over every evening after work, and I'm running on four hours of sleep. I snapped at him yesterday for forgetting his tablets, then sat in the car and cried.
I love him. I also can't do this alone anymore.
Here's what I'm asking. Can you cover half the cost of a daytime attendant? I've found an agency the doctor recommended. Can you video-call him every Sunday so he has something to look forward to? And when you visit in December, can you take the week so I can rest?
I'm not angry at you. I'm tired.
Kiran

qa.q: How long was Baba on the bathroom floor before the neighbour heard him?
qa.a: He was on the floor for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What is Kiran feeling, and what shows it?
qa.a: Kiran feels exhausted and guilty, running on four hours of sleep, snapping at Baba and then crying in the car, while still loving him.

qa.q: Why is Kiran's letter a good way to share the load?
qa.a: It explains calmly, avoids blame, and asks for three concrete things: half the attendant's cost, Sunday calls, and a week of rest in December.

qa.q: What might it be like for Baba to be cared for this way?
qa.a: Baba might feel embarrassed about falling and forgetting, and comforted by Sunday calls to look forward to.

grounding: Shows a young adult balancing time, money and emotions in caring for an ageing parent and asking a sibling to share it.

passage: Vikas, you ask how to talk to your wife's family without starting a war. Let me tell you about my first Diwali after marriage. I, Kalyani, was twenty-five and working at the post office, and my mother-in-law decided I would take ten days' leave to cook for forty relatives. Nobody asked me. I wanted to shout. Instead I waited till the house was quiet, sat beside her while she cut beans, and said, "Amma, I want this Diwali to go well for you. I can take three days, not ten. I'll make the sweets you taught me, and I'll ask my sisters-in-law to share the rest." Her knife stopped. She said nothing for a whole day. Then she told the neighbours, very proudly, that her daughter-in-law made the best adhirasam in the street. She never mentioned the ten days again.

qa.q: How many days of leave did Kalyani agree to take?
qa.a: Three days, not ten.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when the ten days of leave were decided for her?
qa.a: Kalyani felt angry and unheard, wanting to shout because nobody had asked.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Kalyani hold the boundary with respect?
qa.a: Kalyani waited for a calm moment, sat beside the mother-in-law, stated a clear limit of three days, and offered what could be given.

qa.q: How might the mother-in-law have felt during her day of silence?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt or challenged at first, then reassured that Kalyani still cared, which is why she later praised her daughter-in-law proudly.

grounding: An elder recalls holding a respectful boundary with a mother-in-law as a young working wife.

passage:
Sunday, 10 p.m.
Chandrika's big social experiment, week six. Result: I now know four people in this building by name, which is four more than in March.
Today was the potluck I'd been nervous about. I put the note in the lift two weeks ago and was sure nobody would come. Seven people came. Indu from 5B brought lemon rice and her toddler, and stayed to help me wash up. She's a nurse, works nights, and said she's been lonely since moving from Madurai too. We swapped numbers. We've also started a building chat group, just for small things: a spare key, a parcel, someone sick.
It's not a best friend yet. But when my geyser broke last week, I didn't have a single number to call. Now I have four. Slightly proud of myself. Also exhausted. Being social is work.

qa.q: How many people came to the potluck?
qa.a: Seven people came.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel before and after the potluck?
qa.a: Chandrika felt nervous beforehand, sure nobody would come, and afterwards slightly proud but exhausted.

qa.q: What small steps helped Chandrika build a network in the building?
qa.a: Putting a potluck note in the lift, swapping numbers with Indu, and starting a building chat group for everyday help 🙂

qa.q: What might the potluck mean to Indu?
qa.a: Indu has felt lonely since moving from Madurai, so a welcoming neighbour may bring relief and a sense of belonging.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows deliberately building trusted neighbourly ties in a new city.

passage: The grief support group met in a borrowed classroom at the community centre, plastic chairs in a circle. Asif had come three times and said nothing. His father had died in March, and in May the logistics firm let him go in a round of cuts. Most days he woke at noon and scrolled until dark. Tonight Irawati, the facilitator, asked each person for one small thing that had helped that week. When it reached Asif, his throat closed. Then he said, "I made chai at six this morning, the way my father used to. I drank it on the balcony. That's all." Nobody rushed him. "That's not all," Irawati said gently. "That's a routine starting." After the session an older man handed Asif a card for a job-search group that met on Tuesdays. Asif put it in his wallet, next to his father's photo.

qa.q: Where did the grief support group meet?
qa.a: In a borrowed classroom at the community centre.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when it was his turn to speak?
qa.a: He felt grief so heavy that his throat closed, along with a small, shaky hope as he shared the morning chai.

qa.q: How did the group support Asif's recovery?
qa.a: They gave him time without rushing, Irawati named the chai as a routine starting, and a member pointed him to a job-search group.

qa.q: How might Irawati see Asif speaking for the first time?
qa.a: She likely sees it as an important step after three silent sessions and wants him to recognise it as progress.

grounding: Shows a young adult beginning to rebuild routine and support after bereavement and job loss.

passage: The counselling centre's waiting room had a fish tank, and Lokesh always sat facing it, his back to the street window. Eight months after the bus accident, he still flinched at horns and took a longer route to avoid the flyover. He had told everyone he was fine. It was his sister who noticed he had stopped sleeping and booked the first appointment. Inside, Urmila, the counsellor, never pushed him to retell the crash. This week she asked what his body did when he heard a horn. "My chest goes tight. I'm back there." She showed him how to plant his feet, name five things he could see, and breathe slowly. "It doesn't erase it," she said. "It helps you come back to now." On the way home he rode over the flyover. His hands sweated on the handlebar. He did it anyway, and texted his sister: "Took the flyover."

qa.q: How long after the bus accident did Lokesh still flinch at horns?
qa.a: Eight months after the bus accident.

qa.q: What does Lokesh's seat facing the fish tank suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he still felt unsafe and on edge, keeping his back to the street and its noise.

qa.q: What made Urmila's approach helpful?
qa.a: She didn't force him to retell the crash, focused on what his body did, and taught a simple grounding step he could use outside.

qa.q: What might Lokesh's sister feel reading his text?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and proud, having noticed his sleeplessness and booked that first appointment.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising the lasting effects of an accident and healing with a counsellor's support.
